# Scrapwork: R GUI, RStudio, and R code

## Level 1 Growth Model -> Longitudinal Data Analysis

The parentheses just group a recoded time variable. $(\text{AGE} - 11)$ is the slides' version of TIME, and it is 
time-centred at age 11. It isn't a new kind of term, and nothing is being multiplied by anything else. 

### What it does

Define $\text{TIME} = \text{AGE} - 11$. Then:

| AGE | 11 | 13 | 15 |
| --- | -- | -- | -- |
| TIME = AGE - 11 | 0 | 2 | 4 |

So the model is the same Level 1 equation as before, $Y = \pi_0 + \pi_1(\text{TIME}) + \epsilon$, with TIME 
written out as its definition. The subscript $ij$ after the parentheses means the whole quantity can differ by 
person $i$ and occasion $j$, because each teen has their own ages at each wave.

### Why centre at 11 instead of using raw AGE

It changes what the intercept $\pi_{0i}$ means.

With raw AGE, the intercept is the expected delinquency at age 0. That is meaningless, since nobody in the sample 
is 0 and the line would be extrapolated far outside the data. With AGE - 11, the intercept is the expected
delinquency at age 11, the first wave. That is why the slide labels it "initial status", and it is why the arrow 
points to where the dotted line meets age 11 on the plot (about 2).

The slope does not change when you centre. It is still the change in the outcome per year, which is the 
"growth rate" in the second callout.

### Same line, different intercept

Suppose a teen's line is $\text{DelBeh} = 2 + 2(\text{AGE} - 11)$.

- Centred form: intercept = 2 at age 11, slope = 2.
- Expanding it: $2 + 2\text{AGE} - 22 = -20 + 2 \cdot \text{AGE}$, so the uncentred intercept is -20.

These are the same line. An intercept of -20 would imply negative delinquent acts at age 0, which makes no sense, 
so the centred coding is the useful one.

### Choosing where to centre

You can pick any meaningful reference point:

- First wave (AGE - 11): intercept = initial status. This is the usual choice for growth models.
- Midpoint (AGE - 13): intercept = status in the middle of the study.
- Last wave (AGE - 15): intercept = final status.

The choice also changes the variance of the intercepts and the intercept-slope correlation (the random effects), 
so it matters when you interpret those. Fit quality and the slope estimate stay the same.

```r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.cap="Growth trajectories"
setwd("~/Kaggle_Courses/R Programming")

knitr::include_graphics("images/capture.png")

d <- read.csv("yourdata.csv")      # or readxl::read_excel("yourdata.xlsx")
str(d)                             # check the column names

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(
  id    = rep(1:20, each = 3),
  age   = rep(c(11, 13, 15), times = 20)
)
d$time   <- d$age - 11
d$delbeh <- 2 + 2 * d$time + rep(rnorm(20, 0, 1), each = 3) + rnorm(60, 0, 1)

install.packages("lme4")   # once
library(lme4)              # each session, at the top of your Rmd

d$time <- d$age - 11
m1 <- lmer(delbeh ~ time + (1 + time | id), data = d)
```
